name: Japanese thermal reconditioning
lead: Japanese thermal reconditioning, also called yuko or rebonding, is a salon procedure for permanently straightening hair. Wikipedia describes a non-coating chemical applied for about 15 to 20 minutes to loosen cysteine bonds, after which heat restructures the hair into a straight form; the full process takes about four to eight hours.[1]

Because it chemically alters hair structure, new growth is unaffected and grows in with its natural texture.[1] Reported concerns include heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss, and damage from heat is described as irreversible short of cutting the hair off.[1] No clinical studies were found specifically on it.

paras: Wikipedia classes it with permanent chemical methods alongside relaxers, which break disulfide bonds using hydroxide substances.[1] Unlike keratin treatments, which add a coating and last about 6 months, it is described as permanent for the treated hair.[1]
Wikipedia lists heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss for thermal treatments, and chemical burns and breakage for relaxers.[1]

card.summary: Salon chemical-plus-heat process that permanently straightens treated hair; no trials found, heat and scalp damage are reported risks.
card.note: Permanent for treated hair; reported heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss.

quick.overview:
Japanese thermal reconditioning (yuko, rebonding) is a long salon process that uses a chemical to loosen hair bonds and heat to set the hair straight. The result is described as permanent for the treated length.

No clinical studies on it were found.
quick.mechanism: A chemical loosens cysteine bonds in the hair, then heat restructures them in a straight configuration.
quick.risks: Reported risks include heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss; new growth is not straightened.
